en: Master Dongshan’s Way was preeminent in his generation; he looked down upon all quarters with such sternness that students could not approach him at ease, often being driven away by his shouts and rebukes.
Yet this was the very compassion of a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). (Huisheng) once had the honor of serving him and receiving his instructions.
At the time of his passing, the Master entrusted him with his personally edited *yulu* (recorded sayings), all of which...
Deliberating upon the past and present, he brought forth and illuminated what was profound and hidden. Yet, as the monastic robes were finally compiled, the characters "wu" and "yan" had become "ma.

Reflecting on the desire to engrave the corrections so as to broaden its transmission, it is only now that his wish has been fulfilled; this is also in accord with the principle of Ji Zi hanging his sword [as a pledge of sincerity].
Alas! The true Dharma-eye is not like that of ordinary streams. The Elder Dahui always referred to himself by the name Dongshan; now, the Way is being followed.
All who heard it conceived a sense of profound reverence and respect; thus they knew that the bell of Nanyang does not wait for a strike before it resounds.
Written on the first day of the final month of winter in the Wuxu year of the Chunxi era by Ciqiu Huisheng, residing at Leifeng. Respectfully inscribed.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Xuefeng Dongshan of Fuzhou, compiled by his disciple Hui-bi.
After the Master had accepted the invitation and Master Xiufeng had concluded the introductory discourse, the Master ascended the seat. A monk asked: "Before the Master..."

[Question: "What is it like when one sees the thatched hall? The Master said: "There is [one] in Jiangnan. A monk asked: "What is it like after seeing the thatched hall? The Master said: "There is none in Jiangbei.
(The words of thanks are not recorded. The Master then said: "One who is quick-witted acts as soon as they are pointed to."
This dull-witted fellow could not be moved by pushing or pulling; when he walked, everyone rejoiced, but when he did not move, everyone felt resentment.
Now this mountain monk has transformed this dullness into a state of swift agility. (He snaps his fingers once. What was previously unable to be moved is now moved;
what was previously unwilling to dwell in the monastery is now dwelt in; what was previously resentful of the Buddha...

To practice now is to practice. As for what was previously disparaged as "not speaking the Dharma," let us set aside for a moment the questions of whether it emerges or not, whether one abides or not.
I dare ask you all: what kind of Buddha is it that practices? Is it the Buddha of Empty Space (*Ākāśarāja*)? Or is it the Buddha Dīpaṃkara?
"Is it Śākyamuni Buddha? Is it Maitreya Buddha? And what dharma is being taught? Is it the fundamental dharma? Is it the dharma of non-arising?
Is it a worldly dharma? Or is it a supramundane dharma? Is there anyone in this assembly who has realized it?"
"If you can speak thus, this mountain monk’s work in appearing in the world is finished. If it is not yet so, do not err when meeting people.
He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Xiu Feng took leave of the assembly and ascended the hall. Clouds gather in the stone chamber, yet there is originally no mind of expanding or contracting;

beans burst from cold ashes, and thus the distinction between departing and remaining arises. In the ordinary place where we shoulder one another at the rice gruel, the nostrils are seen with the eyes;

when turning the body to breathe through at midnight, the arrow has already passed beyond Silla. Between the two mountains, north and south, the two venerable elders display their elegance—brother calls and brother responds.

The resonance follows the sound and the harmony follows the voice. Furthermore, what does it mean to say, "An arrow has passed over Silla"? How many people can truly know the essential meaning within this?

Entering the monastery, he pointed toward the Abbot’s quarters and said: "From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity down to the present, upon reaching this place, they could do nothing but beg for their lives. All the patch-robed monks under heaven..."
"Monks, when you arrive here, you dare not even breathe. Now tell me, what kind of place is this?
With a shout, he said, "Even Xuefeng’s abbot does not recognize it."

Ascending the seat, he held up the incense. After offering prayers for the Emperor, a monk asked: "Having departed from the Chan monastery on the exquisite peaks, you have come to ascend this sacred site of Xuefeng.
What is the Venerable Immovable One? The Master said: "Walking at night, every step treads upon the bright moon."
The monk said, "In that case, for half a millennium we behold a transcendent person appear, and from ten million heavens the rain of flowers descends.
The Master said, "For a thousand years and ten thousand ages, Mount Xuefeng remains. The monk said, "A master of the school;
his natural state still endures. The Master said, "Thirty years hence, there will not even be a staff left to strike you. After a long silence, he said, "Does the assembly understand?"
A solitary peak like an elephant’s bone; the local lord of Songshan. The oceanic gander’s ninety-thousand-league flight; the Liaodong crane’s three-thousand-year span.
An old guest returning in his declining years to linger in the lingering fragrance. Zhenjue rolling the ball; Xuansha chopping the signboard. Nanquan selling himself; Zhaozhou paying back his debt.
The "tortoise-nose snake" of the Southern Mountains has a head as flat as a fan; if one attempts to grasp it, it will injure the person, for its venom knows no remedy.
The new Elder’s mouth is like a beggar’s straw mat—everything is turned out at once, with nothing more left to conceal or cover.
To use this to honor the Sage, he shall live as long as Heaven and Earth; to use this to bless the Worthy General, he shall be like Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou. With this...
"When the people live in peace and security, the times are clear and the harvests are bountiful. To propagate the Great Teaching in such a manner is to cover heaven and encompass the earth.
Then, he laughed heartily and said, "The moment Empty (Kong) the Elder entered the gate, his mouth was already dripping with water.
What will he be capable of doing in five days? He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
That evening, during the informal sermon (*xiaochan*), a monk asked: "I remember you telling the assembly this morning that previously you could not be pushed or pulled out;
why is it that now you have come out? The Master said: "In a leap year, the spring colors appear late.
The monk asked: "Previously you did not dwell in monasteries; why is it that now you dwell here? The Master said: "In the sixth month, the Yellow River is frozen solid."
The monk said, "In the past, you detested being a Buddha and would not do it;

why do you do it now? The Master said, "What difficulty is there in wearing fur and horns? The monk said, "In the past, you detested preaching the Dharma and would not speak it; why do you speak it now?
The Master said, "In the bitter cold of winter, the iron tree blooms of itself. The monk said, "I thought..."
"The spring has returned, yet there is no place to find it; who would have known it turned its course here? The Master said, "A clumsy fellow!
And off you go again. The Master then addressed the assembly, saying, "For many days, I have been pressed by you all until I could not find a way to die.
I remember that for twenty-one days, the Old Śākyamuni..."
He reflected, saying: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana.
Even this old fellow [Xuefeng], who is not particularly sharp, is still like this; how then can one blame others?
When Xuefeng’s command was issued, there was an old monk whose teeth were like sword-trees and whose mouth was like a blood-basin, holding a white staff and facing it toward Ding... [text fragment].
Standing atop the mountain peak, he waited for the arrival of Xuefeng’s special messenger and his entourage. With a single shout, he brought them to a halt:
"Where do you intend to go? Within the eight prefectures, there are not lacking elders. Why have you crossed mountains and ridges to come here seeking something?
He snatched away the official letter and flung it entirely over the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, followed by a torrent of blows.
At once he struck him back and returned to Pishou Hall. There, this mountain monk spread out his sitting mat and paid him nine prostrations, honoring him as his teacher.
Now that I lack such skillful means, I cannot help but don the fur and wear the horns [of an animal];
I cast my body across the sea of right and wrong and move with ease through the midst of a pack of jackals and tigers. *He lets out a shout.*
The Master descended from his seat and ascended the hall. A monk asked: "You strike the Dharma drum that is about to fall, and you shake the profound net that has already collapsed.
Now that the Dharma drum has sounded and the profound net has been shaken, I wonder: is there anything extraordinary within the sound of the drum? The Master said: "There is."
The monk asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said, "Yangqi saw Ciming. The monk said, "I do not yet understand;
I beg the Master to point it out again. The Master said, "Yun'an studied under Jicui.
The monk said, "As for Heshan’s four drumbeats, by which the entire assembly attained awakening—how does that compare with the Master’s sounding of the drum? Are they the same or different?"
The Master said, "Have you attained realization yet? The monk said, "I, this student, have attained realization.

The Master said, "You are mocking the old man in your own house! The Master then said, "Excellent, great assembly! To attain such essentiality and such manifest presence—therefore, as the ancients said:
'If among a thousand or ten thousand people there were but one who could truly and thoroughly realize it, I would carry him on my back.'"
When a monk acts as a donkey carrying goods to provide for others, what fault or transgression is there? Ancient worthies were not without good intentions;

they simply chose monks to bestow gifts upon and selected Buddhas to offer incense to. I observe this assembly: among these thousands and hundreds of people, there is not a single one who does not possess great resolve.
Therefore, from the moment I received the summons from the Prefect at Xiufeng, I immediately donned these sheepskin robes.
What is it that the camel carries? How does one make offerings? Is there anyone who can see it?
After a long silence, he said: "In the morning there is porridge, at mealtime there is rice;
day after day incense and flowers, night after night lamps."

Ascending the hall to address the new officers of the two orders: As soon as this mountain monk arrived at Xueling, he forged an iron boat without a bottom and launched it into the sea of True Awakening, to transport both the sentient and the insentient, teaching them not to dwell on this shore nor to linger on the other shore.
Not remaining in the middle current, each one emerges and acts like a true monk:

Mañjuśrī holds the oar at the head, Samantabhadra holds the rudder to straighten the tail, the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Bodhisattva rows the sweeps on both sides, and the Non-Retrogressive Bodhisattvas watch the wind and set the sails.
This mountain monk knows only to wash his feet and board the boat; he eats a single meal at midday and sleeps at night.
One night’s stay. When the smoke has vanished and the sun rises, heaven and earth are vast; with a single cry of "kuan-erh," the mountains and waters turn green. Good brother!
Upon ascending the seat at Dongchan, after the questions were finished, the Master said: "The mountain tortoise has its shell; it considers itself secure and happy for the rest of its life."
While he was in the mire, many hands attacked him; this was indeed due to Fenggan’s loquaciousness.

From the very beginning, it caused him to hide his head while exposing his tail, or hide his tail while exposing his head, turning left and right to evade in every way, yet none could catch him. One day, suddenly and unexpectedly, he was cornered.
In a single moment, he cast off his skin and shell, leaving himself completely bare. Taking this wretched life of his, he threw it forth with all his heart before the assembly;
yet, there was not a single thing remaining. He then laughed heartily and said, "Do not say that being 'without affairs' is good."

Ever since leaving the mountains, I have been arranging a certain essential teaching of Chan. Upon arriving at Dongsi Temple, I faced the Great Master and discussed matters from east to west with various elders for several days.
However, as I attended to the affairs of state and people rolled in one after another, today, when I arrived here and felt about my own chest, I could not remember a single word.
How much less can I speak of the "Three Gates" or the "Five Gates"? Even this one gate is beyond me.
It will do. One day at Wangzhou Pavilion or Wushan Ridge, we shall meet unexpectedly; do not say that I have let you off now.

(When Minister Li invited the Master to the Xiaoyun Hermitage, the Master did not go out. Dongchan sent a verse to the Master which said: "The mountain tortoise has its shell to hide its head and tail; even seventy-two drills, what can they do? And so forth.")
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: One day, Zhenjue asked the mendicant Bei, "Why do you not go to visit various teachers?
Bei replied, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land; the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Zhenjue approved of this.

Having finished citing the case, the Master let out a great laugh and said, "Later on, those in the monastic communities all claimed these words were extraordinary, yet they did not realize that this old fellow had reached..."
Now, beneath this stupa, they sit in dense clusters. It was simply because of such behavior at that time.
If anyone were to say today, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven," they would immediately be struck with a staff and driven out.
Why was he accepted at that time? Yet now, he is beaten and driven from the monastery. Those with eyes to see should discern this.
Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: The hundred rivers flow in different directions, yet all return to the sea; the myriad regions distinguish various meanings, yet they all culminate in reality.

Therefore, the traveling monks from the ten directions gather together for the summer retreat on the Snowy Mountains. Among them, there are those who have already attained realization and those who have not;

there are those who study the doctrines and those who study the profound mysteries. Yet none of them fail to take Great Perfect Enlightenment as their monastery, dwelling peacefully within body and mind, free from distraction.
"Without soil. He then gave a shout and said, "Now tell me: does this one shout function as a shout, or does it not function as a shout?
Is it a probing pole or a blade of grass? Is it the Vajra King’s precious sword? Is it a crouching lion?

Those who have not yet attained the eye that penetrates the barrier—do not say you have no doubts. (Having finished his introductory remarks,) he then said, "The ancients said: 'Not yet reaching the bottom.'"
People, investigating the words is not as good as investigating the meaning; for one who has reached the bottom, attaining the meaning is not as good as attaining the words.

The ancients acted thus to accommodate the present age; even in that which is not elegant, there is elegance of its own. You younger practitioners who enter the assembly to study Chan must be meticulous;
you must not engage in empty pretension. First, you must attain awakening; once awakened, you must practice.
Once you have set out, you must penetrate thoroughly; once you have penetrated, you will be like a true monk, for whom nothing is considered extraordinary.

This mountain monk is a hundredfold ugly and a thousandfold clumsy; my speech is dull and unrefined, and I have no fresh phrases to offer—no gathering of flowers or clustering of brocade, no four-six or eight-six parallel couplets to regale you, brothers.
It is simply a single mouthful of the wondrous, sharp blade of wisdom. To anyone who comes before it, there is no... [respite].
"Eliminate one blow. Moreover, how can you enter the gate of Xuefeng? [The Master] let out a shout and descended from the seat.

On the occasion of the Summer Retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "Nine years at Shaoshi—waiting for a rabbit by guarding a tree stump. Three prostrations by Shen Guang—seeking fish by climbing a tree."
“Mazu’s ‘The mind itself is Buddha’ is wrong from the very start. Panshan’s ‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ is still off the mark at the end.
Linji’s shouting as soon as one enters the gate is far too frantic. Deshan’s striking as soon as one enters the gate has not yet met a true master.”
Zhaozhou’s “Gate” is a forced fabrication; Huishan’s “Water-Ox” is enough to put people to shame. Yunmen’s “Looking at the Mirror” is merely commonplace;
Xuefeng’s “Rolling the Ball” remains unresolved even to this day. All these are matters from the past that could not be brought to a final conclusion.
This has caused subsequent generations to be burdened by its legacy. Now, is there anyone under Xuefeng who transcends past and present, who is peerless and beyond compare?
On the fifteenth day of the summer retreat, bring forth a single phrase!
Even if you could speak it, it would still be like losing money in a river and searching for it in the same river. (He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.)
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Scholars, Anfu, made offerings to the Sangha and requested the Master to ascend the hall.
A monk asked, "In the past, Prime Minister Li visited Yaoshan and asked, 'What is the Way? Yaoshan replied, 'Clouds in the blue sky, water in the jar.

What is the meaning of this principle? The Master said, "A fragrant breeze comes from the south. The monk said, "As it turns out, there is not much to this single phrase; its strategic application is still [to be seen]."
The monk asked, "When he first arrived at the monastery, the Master said, 'Grasses and trees emit a radiant glow.
The monk continued, 'As for what the Minister said—refining his physical form until it resembles that of a crane, with two cases of scriptures beneath a thousand pine trees;
when I came to ask about the Way, there was no further teaching—'Clouds in the blue sky, water in the jar. How about this? The Master said, "A single character enters the gate of officialdom."

"Nine oxen cannot pull it out. The monk said, "It truly causes the heroic spirit of a thousand years to stir throughout the world; it remains scattered throughout the monastic communities to this day. The Master said, "Passing through the marketplace with one's body turned sideways; walking while looking up at the heavens. The monk said: [The Master] said: "Nine oxen cannot pull it out. The monk said:

"It truly causes the heroic spirit of a thousand years to stir throughout the world; it remains scattered throughout the monastic communities to this day. The Master said: "Passing through the marketplace with one's body turned sideways; walking while looking up at the heavens. The monk said: [silence].
One might say that a fine breeze comes without end; its true illumination and function are inexhaustible.

The Master said, "Truly so. He then continued: "The single source of all spirits is named Buddha. Its radiance soars through past and present, utterly transcending seeing and knowing. It is perfectly full throughout the ten voids."
It certainly has a specific location. To be deluded regarding it is to become a sentient being; to awaken to it is to become a Buddha.

Although there appears to be a distinction between the born (sentient beings) and the Buddha, this fundamental reality is inherently without increase or decrease. Abiding in heaven, one is heaven; dwelling among humans, one is human. Among bhikṣus, one is the most honored among bhikṣus;
among lay practitioners, one is the most honored among lay practitioners; among women, one is [the most honored] among women.
The most honored among those of middle rank; among officials, he is the most honored among officials. Wherever he may be, he is always supreme. [The Master] then raised his whisk and said:
"Now, upon the tip of this mountain monk’s whisk—what would you call it?
If you can carry this burden here, do not dare to bring it forth before a patch-robed monk. But tell me, what else does a patch-robed monk possess?"
Regarding this point, I recall how the Imperial Secretary Yang Yi asked Guanghui: "I have heard the Master say that all sinful karma arises from wealth and treasures;
you therefore advise people to distance themselves from them. Yet, in this Jambudvīpa, sentient beings take wealth as their very lifeblood, and states gather their people through wealth.
In the teachings, there are two kinds of giving: the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma. How [is this to be reconciled]?"
Dawang Dequan said to someone who was being urged to distance themselves from wealth: "The iron dragon-head on the tip of the banner pole. The Shilang (Court Gentleman) replied:
"The sea-monster horse is as large as a donkey. Daquan said: "A chicken of Chu is not the phoenix of Mount Dan. The Shilang said:

"Two thousand years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and yet bhikṣus have little sense of shame. [Daquan said: "O Great Assembly! You monks of Chan, when you are questioned in your daily lives, your mouths are like—"
Spinning wheel. Do you know where these two men have fallen? Today, not sparing my eyebrows, I shall celebrate and praise for the sake of this meal, speaking to all of you:
Xuefeng was invited by Minister Zhang; thirty years hence, do not misrepresent this.
The donor distributed the scriptures and requested that the Master ascend the hall. "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and signs are quiescent.

If the Old Man Śākyamuni had been able to take even a single step here, he would have expounded the entire Great Canon for forty-nine years upon the Vulture Peak assembly, filling the Dragon Palace and the Sea Treasury, and circulating throughout the heavens and the human world. Master Bodhidharma—
Look here! If you can gain even a single eye, you will understand why [the Master] traveled all the way from South India, ten thousand *li*, to arrive here at Shaolin;
why he sat facing the wall for nine years; and how he transmitted the mind-seal alone, without establishing written words.
If the old monks of the world can emerge from this point with a head above the crowd, they will understand how to spread the Great Dharma upon a bed of crooked wood and rope.
The Teaching flows forth from the breast, covering heaven and earth; it is divided into three sections, and now we come to the first.
[He raises his staff and says: "In a single stroke, they are all pierced through. [He strikes once and says: "Where have they gone? (Having finished the introductory remarks, he continues:
"If birth and death exist, from antiquity until today, no one has been able to escape them. If birth and death do not exist, from antiquity until today..."
Now, no one can escape it. Whether birth and death are both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent—in all such cases, there is none who can escape them.
Since this is so, how then can one escape? There is only this single word: "Awakening."
Apart from this, there is no gate; apart from this, there is no path.

If you all were suddenly to awaken right where you stand, do not even speak of birth and death—down to the empty space of the ten directions, it would all utterly vanish. I fear only that your faculties and thoughts may falter and hesitate.
You have not yet been able to glimpse liberation. I, this mountain monk, shall give you a parable. It is like a person who has fallen asleep; his body is upon the bed, secure and at ease.
Suddenly, without cause, he sees within a dream a venomous snake and a fierce tiger vying to devour him.
His heart is filled with dread, and in frantic terror he runs away. While in the very midst of his flight, suddenly his eyes open. And so it is born.

The nature of death is also like this. Suddenly, there was a monk who came forward and said, "How is it that the Elder Xuefeng, having received such offerings from a donor, speaks on the Dharma seat nothing but a dream?
He then laughed heartily and said, "So, one must not speak of dreams in front of a fool."
When Master Dongchan arrived, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "O Great Assembly! A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is like the nectar of heaven;
some may merely hear its name but do not get to drink it. A spiritual friend is like rain during a drought; some may merely long for it but do not receive its moisture.
A spiritual friend is like the Vajra King’s precious sword; if there are those who behold it, their thieving mind is forever severed."
A man of knowledge is like a lion at the gateway; those who behold him find their doubts forever stilled.
Today, this mountain gate is most fortunate to receive the arrival of the Great Zen Master, the Abbot of Dongchan, whose majestic carriage has graced us.
To this mountain monk and the entire assembly, it is as if we have drunk nectar or obtained sweet rain in our thirst; how much more so since the Zen Master is an old friend of mine.
For thirty years on the rivers and lakes, this has been known to every monastery; there is no need to speak of it further.

There is only one matter that must be exposed before the assembly: placing a thousand-and-five-hundred-pound iron cangue upon this mountain monk’s neck was precisely this old fellow’s "poisonous hand.
Last night, within the abbot’s quarters, he showed all manner of paternal care and gave all manner of instruction, as if—
The great axe has struck; he rubs his hands together. Now, we can only joyfully endure it.

Upon descending from the seat, he immediately joins the administrators and the assembly in extending a formal invitation to ascend this throne, so that the present congregation may know that the Vajra King Linji and the Lion at the Gate Fenyang—the bell and hammer of the successive sages and the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—remain unbroken to this day.
Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Patriarch’s death: Old Man [Linji] practiced Zen with such great hardship—nine times he went up to Dongshan and three times to Touzi.
Under Deshan’s staff, the bottom of the bucket fell away; at the head of the Ao-shan shop, it was of no further use.

From the time he attained the Way until now, the "tortoise-nose" has injured people, and there is no medicine for its poison. There is no medicine for its poison—but fortunately, at that time, he lacked one thing. But tell me, what did he lack?

First point: Today is the anniversary of the passing of the founding patriarch, Zen Master Jingue. Since the mountain gate has restricted its days and rationed its food, matters no longer compare to those of old.
This mountain monk cannot help but turn what is non-existent into something existent, merely to ensure that the family reputation does not fall.
Thus, I take ten billion sets of four continents as a single ritual altar, and ten billion Mount Sumerus as a single plate of sour minced meat.
She took ten billion sets of four continents as a single bowl of *bōtóu* (boiled noodles) and ten billion suns and moons as a single table setting of lamps and candles.
Although her offerings were meager, they were not sought from without. She immediately rose and performed a woman’s bow, saying:
"May Master Zeng be ever blessed; please do not take offense at my lack of refinement."
Ascending the hall, Xuefeng said on the fifth day of the fifth month: "Without relying on divine talismans or wondrous arts, there is only a single blow from the crown of the head.
He then planted his staff in the ground and said: "Even an iron Buddha must break into a sweat."

The patron requested a universal discourse. The Master said: "If one speaks, it is not universal; if it is universal, one does not speak. If there is anything spoken, it is ultimately not a universal discourse.
Flowers blooming in an ice cave, snow falling from a scorching sky—those with clear eyes and high standing must well discern the timing.
Tell me, what is the present moment? Is it the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m. at dusk? Is it the time when lamps and candles shine together?"
"Have humans and devas gathered here in such numbers? If it is so, you have missed the proper time and occasion by no small measure.

Tonight, three female lay disciples have invited me for a general discourse on their behalf, to pray for the longevity of the Great Lady. He then recalled how the King of Min once asked Chan Master Shoushan about his age.
The King asked, "How old are you, Master Shou? Shou replied, "I am as long-lived as empty space. The King asked, "How old is empty space? Shou replied, "It is..."
"Longevity Mountain shares the same longevity [as the sky]. The Master said, "Longevity Mountain is indeed extraordinary; yet it is old and decrepit.

It cannot distinguish between master and servant, nor differentiate between jade and stone. It knows only that it shares the same longevity as empty space, but it fails to realize that empty space is actually its own descendant."
Lingxi requested the assembly to ascend the hall. "The Buddhas of the three periods cannot show their heads here;
the entire Great Canon of Teachings cannot inscribe a single character here. The mouths of the teachers throughout the world are shattered into a hundred fragments here.
This is the Dharma spoken by Master Zhengjue three hundred years ago; even until today, it has not shifted by so much as a hair’s breadth. Nevertheless, so it is."
True awakening only knows how to hold fast; it does not know how to let go into practice.

Today, because Lingxi has established a vegetarian feast for the opening of the sutras, I shall grant a single thread of the Way, allowing it to shine with brilliant radiance everywhere. Raising his staff, he said:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time sit here upon the precious lotus flower, realize equal and perfect enlightenment, and preach the Dharma to deliver all beings."
Within this great treasury of the teachings, the meaning of every character is radiant; in every word, one perceives the Truth. There is no need for further translation.
Regarding this very point, the teachers of the world—whether speaking much or little, whether explaining vertically or horizontally—have nothing remaining that has not been fully expressed.

He then laughed heartily and said: "When the Great Statue of Jiazhou hears such talk, it will suddenly transform into Kāśyapa and take the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the western continent of Aparagoyānī, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru, binding them together into a single brush.
With this, he will write seven characters in the great void of space, saying: 'The Great Sutra of Vairocana’s Dharma-Jewel.'"
[This] scroll: those in the world with eyes cannot see it; those with mouths cannot recite it.
Only the fifteen hundred patch-robed monks in the Snow Peak mountains can each see it and recite it.
If you do not believe this, I, the mountain monk, shall further speak a verse for you: "The Great Man above, Qiu Yi Ji; transformed three thousand, seventy scholars; you..."
"I have eight or nine children; when they are well-raised and benevolent, one can know their propriety. [The Master] descends from his seat.

At the request of Lingxi for a general discourse (*pushe*), the Master says: "For many days now, I have struck the drum to enter the hall for formal sermons, small-scale instructions (*xiaocan*), and general discourses.
Look at my tongue in my mouth—is it there? He then opens his mouth wide and asks, "Is it there? If you say it is there—
They continue to deceive the men and women of this world without end. Even if one says they are worn out, they still deceive the men and women of this world without end.
I, this mountain monk, now depart from them in a different way. You all must tonight establish a different eye for yourselves; only then will it suffice.

At the request of Xianglin Temple, he ascended the hall. "The Great has no exterior; the Small has no interior.

With neither interior nor exterior, throughout the seven locations and nine assemblies, whether saintly or ordinary, all are layered and unimpeded. To twist the nostrils and shatter Mount Sumeru—" then, raising his staff, he said:
"Look, look! The people of Magadha in Western India see you Zen practitioners in the midst of Xuefeng Mountain."
"Disciples, practicing Chan is no easy matter. Generally speaking, from the tip of this mountain monk’s staff, I shall perform the *Yunshao* melody as an offering for you all;
furthermore, I shall recite for you the *Siddhārthapratāraṇa*, the supreme divine mantra:

'The ox of Huai Prefecture eats the grain; The horse of Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly. Seeking a physician throughout the world, One applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. Then he laughed heartily."
He laughed loudly and said, "I thought he was a man from Magadha; it turns out he is merely the Venerable Dushun.
He struck his staff once. Again, he raised [the case]: An outsider asked the Buddha, "I do not ask about words, nor do I ask about wordlessness. The World-Honored One remained seated.
The outsider praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One, in your great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away my clouds of delusion and enabled me to attain [enlightenment]."
He entered, prostrated, and departed. Ānanda asked, "What did that outsider see that he prostrated, offered praise, and then left?

The World-Honored One said, "He was like a fine horse that moves at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip. The Great Assembly: "At this moment, this mountain monk does not take his seat for a long while;
nor does he manifest great kindness and great compassion, nor does he clear away your clouds of delusion. Is there anyone who can enter?"
"Dima! He then gave a shout and said, "One must not entirely adopt the views and interpretations of the non-Buddhists.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The followers of the Chan school can see what is truly seen; they can speak what is truly spoken. In the subtlety of speech, the mountain monk is no match for them;
in the sharpness of the spiritual pivot, the mountain monk does not equal them. Since he is neither a match nor an equal, why does he say, 'He has not yet attained it'?"
If you do not comprehend this meaning, your practice will be nothing but bitter toil.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Every dharma is the original dharma; there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Why, within a single dharma, would there be dharma and non-dharma?
Above is heaven, below is earth—what is the 'original dharma'? When hungry, there is food; when weary, there is sleep."

When it is hot, one seeks coolness wherever it may be found; when it is cold, one returns to the quarters to face the fire. Why, within a single Dharma, should there be both what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma?
My mountain monk’s commentary in this manner must surely provoke the laughter and wonder of those with clear eyes. Since I have opened this door...
As long as people can laugh, today—the first day of the tenth month—I shall provide a brazier for you within this small cell.
I do not dare hope that you will turn the Great Dharma Wheel while sitting amidst the flames; I simply wait for the moment when you fall asleep.
Only when his nostrils are scorched will he finally find it laughable. He lets out a shout and says, "Laugh at what?
Ascending the hall, he picks up his staff and says, "The Great Master Yunmen said: 'Ordinary people truly say it exists; those of the Two Vehicles analyze it and say it does not exist;
Pratyekabuddhas call it illusory existence; Bodhisattvas see its very substance as emptiness. As for the monk, when he sees the staff..."
"Staff. [The Master] merely called it a "walking staff. When walking, one simply walks; when sitting, one simply sits. One must not move it at all.
Having finished speaking, the Master laughed heartily and said: "This is where Great Master Yunmen looked upon you, the monks of the world, as children.
Since he has arranged you in such a manner, he further forbids you from moving. How vexing! Thereupon, he struck the ground with his staff.
He struck the ground once with his staff, held it up, and said: "Ordinary people, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Zen monks—all have been pierced through at once by Yunmen.
Those who can move it, go ahead and move it. He threw down the staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "When a single bubble arises from the deep ocean, its clarity remains undisturbed to the very bottom.

Floating upon the sea amidst appearing and disappearing, creation and destruction come and go in the snap of a finger. [The Master] took up the whisk and said: "Having grasped this, at such a time as this, when a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?
The Master said: "The assembly shall bear witness. The monk said: "If so, then it is according to one's lot."
[The monk] said, "I am going to put on my clothes and eat my meal; there is nothing else to do. The Master asked, "Where did you see the deceased monk?
The monk replied, "Throughout the entire world he cannot escape his physical form; upon a single hair-tip, his whole body appears. The Master said:
"Not a few deceased monks have been buried," [the monk] said. The monk continued, "I recall Xuansha asking Master Zhenjue, 'When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?
Zhenjue replied, 'It is like ice returning to water. Xuansha did not approve. Zhenjue then asked him, 'And what about you?
Xuansha said, 'It is like water returning to ice. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "In total..."
A monk asked, "What is the phrase for being free and easy? The Master said, "The Damu Creek at the head of the Iron Chain Bridge.
The monk bowed. The Master said, "If you understand this as being 'free and easy,' you will enter hell like a shooting arrow.
The Master then said, "Dongshan said: 'When the weather is clear, cover the house; when the time comes, reap the grain. [He] delivered it..."
The king’s taxes have been paid; they drum their bellies and sing songs of praise. When the ancients lived in the mountains, they were able to settle matters so thoroughly and enjoy such happiness.
Yet Xuefeng had a roof that was not yet finished, grain that was not yet harvested, and taxes that remained unpaid.
Just as we were waiting for him to drum his belly and sing songs of joy, Yidu Zhuang has also passed away.
How bitter! I venture to ask the assembly: all are equally those who have left the household life; all are equally mountain-dwellers. Why, then, do their suffering and joy differ?
Do you understand? "The waves at Caoxi are just like this; countless ordinary people are submerged beneath them. (He lets out a shout. He descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Bending one’s head, one does not see the earth; looking up, one does not see the sky. If you wish to know the place of the white ox, simply look before the skull.
He struck the ground with his staff toward the east and said: "Master Zhenjue stands here on this side.

The single path that transcends all is not transmitted by the thousand sages; students weary their bodies, like a monkey grasping at reflections. He struck the ground with his staff toward the west and said:
Panshan Worthy stands here. *Du! Du! Du!* His power is rare. The Zen students are startled; his eyebrows hang down.
Striking the ground with his staff in the center, he says: "Yunmen Worthy stands here. These three old fellows—
Now tell me, who today deserves to eat Xuefeng’s Hu-pie? Let those who can discern it try to discern it for Xuefeng.
As for the principles of the Three Mysteries, they are certainly not a panacea for all ailments. "A single word that is not mysterious—such a fellow is but a worldly teacher.
Having said this, he descended from his seat and went on a tour of the quarters to question the brothers; there were many who offered responses. The Master said:
"There are many people who have mouths but cannot eat *hūbǐng* (barley cakes).
He ascended the hall and raised the following case: Master Dongshan addressed the assembly, saying, "You must know that there is a matter beyond the Buddha. A monk then asked:
"What is the matter that transcends [the Buddha]? Shanshan said, "Not a Buddha. Master Yunmen said, "It cannot be named;
it cannot be described. That is why he said 'not. Later, Old Man Miaoxi said, 'It is not so here with me.
What is the matter that transcends the Buddha? I would grab my staff and strike him across the spine, lest he remain stuck on his heels looking upward toward the Buddha.'"
The Great Assembly at Dongshan opened their mouths wide, yet in the end they could not close them; when questioned by others, they could only manage to say "not Buddha" with all their might.
Furthermore, there was the lame master Yunmen, who lacked integrity and instead followed the perverse and pursued the evil.
Only Miaoxi is slightly better. Upon closer inspection, his staff lacks some firmness.
These three old fellows may serve as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), but regarding the matter that transcends the Buddha, they have not yet seen even a dream of it.
Is there anyone present now who has seen a dream? [He lets out a shout. He descends from the seat.

Ascending the hall: Before a single bubble has arisen, before the ancient sail has been hoisted, before the wind’s signal has arrived, and before anyone has raised the oars—precisely at such a time, how can one discern it?
Suddenly, if there is a man who, looking here, sees through it all, and then comes to observe the world, what a marvelous performance this is!
This marvelous performance: if he is at home, he acts as a youth; if he is...
A person who leaves the household life becomes a bhikṣu through ascetic practice. If one is deluded regarding this, one is deluded and enters the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence;
if one awakens to it, one awakens and becomes a Buddha or a Bodhisattva. In the state of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there is no increase;
in the four modes of birth and the six realms, there is no decrease. In the bhikṣu, there is no superiority; in ascetic practice, there is no inferiority. Since this is so—
"Inferior, not superior; neither increasing nor decreasing. Then, picking up his staff, he said:
"Why does this staff come forth, pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, declaring: 'In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored'? Do you understand? After a long silence, he said:
"A family prospers through filial sons; a state achieves hegemony through strategic ministers.
Thus, when the practitioner Gan-zhi prepared congee at Nanquan, Nanquan struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the cat and the white ox.
Gan-zhi bowed and departed. After the assembly had left the hall, they asked the kitchen steward, "Where has the practitioner Gan-zhi gone?"
"Where was he? the Master asked. The attendant replied, "At that time, he prostrated and went out immediately. Nanquan then smashed the rice porridge pot.

This public case has been tasted by practitioners everywhere, yet it is like chewing raw iron. Today, because an attendant prepared rice porridge, I have brought this out in verse for the great assembly:
"The wildcat and the white ox recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; Ganqi and Nanquan do not differ much. The rice porridge pot is smashed!"
Where has the cauldron gone? Amidst the howling winds and rains of the empty mountains at night.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Xuefeng established a quarters that had already fallen into disuse, restoring it to its former name. I recall Chan Master Fayan saying:
'Simply continue as before in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; in dressing and eating; in morning attendance and evening requests—in all things, continue as before.'"
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas attain [enlightenment] within the state of remaining as they are. I venture to ask the great assembly: what is it that they have attained?

If there is something attained, then one does not remain as they are; if there is nothing attained, one likewise does not remain as they are. If one attains non-attainment, taking non-attainment as attainment, then one even more certainly does not remain as they are.
Now, if you wish to remain as you are, first take up Master Fayan’s single blow.
"Beat him to death! Give him to the dogs to eat! Then, with a single pull, he knocked down the signboard he had erected and threw it onto a heap of refuse.
Only then did he enter this cell and "plant fields in the ears" and "grow vegetables at the feet of the beds" for the eight Zen guests.
Although they were not yet true masters, let the rector be pleased. Thus does the mountain monk act.
For people, it is like picking up a mouthful to drink water. Entering the hall, [the Master said]:
"Śākyamuni appeared in the world carrying snow to fill a river; Bodhidharma came from the West hoping to plant trees among the clouds.
Since then, Mazu, Shitou, Deshan, Linji, and all the old monks under heaven have been riding on emptiness and responding to echoes, vying with one another to show their heads."
Come! To speak of mind and nature, to strike with the staff, and to shout—these are all heroes of a chaotic age, rogues in a time of peace.
Within the domain of a patch-robed monk, none of these are of any use. But tell me, what does a patch-robed monk ordinarily employ? Today is the first day of the month;
I shall now descend from the seat and briefly visit the various quarters to inquire after you.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised up the case of Yaoshan, who said: "I have a phrase; I will speak it when a hornless ox gives birth to a calf.
Later, Yuanjian said: "I have a phrase; I will speak it when a tongueless person asks for it. These two venerable elders—
One might say that "the fat do not reveal the flesh, and the thin do not reveal the bone. This is indeed so, yet it seems somewhat too profound.
I, this mountain monk, am not like this. I have a single phrase: when you open your mouth, you see my gallbladder. This is indeed so, yet it seems somewhat too shallow and mundane.
If you can gain realization under the words of these two elders, then "when you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not beat it to death. If you can gain realization under my words...
"Recommended! Entering hell is like being shot by an arrow. [He lets out a shout.

He descends from his seat. Ascending the hall: "When this mountain monk entered the city, there were three extraordinary matters. Today, having returned, I have struck the drum and ascended the hall."
He presented these matters to the assembly: "First, the waters of the Southern Terrace River pass through the nostrils of Fangshan.
Second, the Wansui Pagoda and the Baoren Pagoda vie for prominence at the brow. Third, before the mountain, Old Man Li rides a lame donkey out from beneath the Drum Gate, crying, 'Look at the horse!
Look at the horse! Yet the mountain monk sits cross-legged within his sedan chair. He then recalled Dongshan’s verse:
The Master said: "The entire Great Canon of the Teachings is merely this single character 'zhi' (之). This alone is what I report to you; I humbly hope you will understand.
When Chan Master Guangxiao arrived, he ascended the hall. A monk asked: "At Elephant Bone Rock, the heights are places where men do not go;

those who do go must be those with the skillful hands of a snake-handler. How many masters such as Linji and Xuefeng have been rendered helpless, losing their very bodies and lives? Now that we have encountered [this situation]..."
[The monk] arrived. “I do not know, Reverend, how you will receive me? The Master said, “Boil tea with water from the mountain stream;
burn firewood from the cave to heat the cauldron. The monk said, “In that case, I shall drink a bowl of coarse tea and listen to some plain talk about the sound of rain.
The Master said, “Excessive ritual leads to confusion. The monk said, “I remember Yaoshan saying, ‘I have a single phrase.’”
"I will tell you as soon as the special ox gives birth. Now it has been born; please, Master, speak. The Master said:
"The skin on his face is not even three inches thick. The monk said: "When the Master speaks, he speaks too much.
But the student is still not satisfied. The Master said: "Advancing forward, one is entirely unaware; retreating backward, one begins to feel sorrow. The monk said: "Perfect Mirror."
The Master said, "I have a single phrase. I will speak it when someone without a tongue asks. But how about that?
The monk asked, "Master, you once said, 'I have a single phrase; open your mouth and you shall see the food.
Why is it, then, so difficult to understand? The Master said, "If you could understand it, I would break your staff."
The monk said, "Is it not the case that everything is already so? The Master struck him and then said: "Great fields are shrouded in clouds;
a thousand peaks are cold with hue. Flying geese sever the path; the ancient road is hard to ascend.

I did not expect that the Zen Master from Guangxiao Hall would raise high the banner of the Dharma from afar to visit this desolate place. My feelings of gratitude are beyond words. He then descended from his seat.
You should join the administrative assembly in extending this formal invitation for you to ascend this seat and fulfill the hopes of the multitude.
As the ancients said: "If one wishes to find a man of exceptional talent, he must possess four qualities to fully manifest the path of a patriarchal master:
first, the nostrils of the ancestral teachers; second, the adamantine eye; third, the claws and fangs of a lion; and fourth, the patched robe."

The monk’s staff is the means by which life and death are governed. Having attained these four matters, one may manifest transformations in every direction, rolling up and unfolding at will, towering above gods and humans, standing like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
If one fails to harmonize with this, yet clings to death while claiming to follow the Good Path, it is a sign of a defeated army.
For a Chan Master—a veteran general of the Dharma-gate and a true son of the Buddha-Sun—these four matters are simply his daily fare. His...
The Zen practitioners in the Xuefeng Mountains may not yet have heard this. I prostrate myself and humbly hope that you will not withhold your compassion, but deign to extend a single hand.
At the small *can* (sermon) on the night of the winter solstice, he took up his staff, struck it once, and said: "The great pavilion of Vairocana—eight characters. He struck it again.
It is opened! Whether you are a long-time practitioner or a beginner, come forth for the communal labor. Once you enter, all enters; once it is finished, all is finished.
Thus, one can sit and cut off the crown of Vairocana, receiving no instructions from Śākyamuni.
At such a time, Maitreya withdraws his body to clear the way, and Xuefeng keeps his mouth shut while eating his meal. Why? It is because all of you are like this.
It is realized as it truly is. One enters according to reality, understands according to reality, and sees according to reality.

The use of "this mind is Buddha" is not applicable; the use of "neither mind nor Buddha" is not applicable. The five ranks and three paths cannot be employed; Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout are not applicable.
As long as there are words and explanations, none of them are applicable. Since they are not applicable, they cannot even be spoken of.
It is attained. Tonight, Xuefeng will ring the bells and beat the drums to assemble everyone; it cannot simply end like this.

"The Buddha is the mind" or "the Buddha is not the mind"—throughout the ages, this has been clear and manifest, nothing other than this. This very true mind is my own mind, yet even my own mind emerges from provisional skillful means.
Whether through the five ranks or the three paths, these are established as skillful, reciprocal adjustments according to the capacity of the occasion. Not...
Contact is the very root of our own school. Extending the hand, one penetrates the mystery; Buddhas and patriarchs vanish.

Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout emerge alone from the universe, sweeping across all with a horizontal stroke. From beginning to end, who dares to make arbitrary distinctions? The talkative old master cannot speak of it.
As for what was before, it could not be used and could not be spoken of. As for what was after, it could be spoken of and could be used.
Is this because the tongue has no bone? Is this because one who has attained the Way finds that the fire does not burn the mouth?
Is this because I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas? If it were so, you would merely be lodging in a grass hut, staying outside the gate.

He then leaned on his staff and said: "I am but a simple and unrefined man, unfit for such a task; I ought to have remained in a mountain cave. Yet, as my karmic ties were not yet exhausted, I have accepted this humble office here.

From spring through summer, and now until the winter solstice, I have relied upon my fellow practitioners and brothers in charge who, with sincerity and all their strength, have together raised the banner of the Dharma.
I am also indebted to the brothers who have come from afar, who have endured hunger and plain food to share in this Way."
The Dharma-gate is in decline; there has never been a time more critical than this. We rely entirely upon you, brothers of lofty aspiration and vision, to come forth and together restore it.
This is my most earnest longing. Deep within the Snow Peak mountains, the cold is bitter and the silence is profound.
Today there are some fruits, yet I cannot wait for nightfall; I have already eaten them first. I only remember this.
While Dongshan was eating fruit with the Head Seat Tai, Dongshan said, "There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth;
it is as black as lacquer. It is ever present within activity, yet it cannot be contained within activity. Now tell me, where does its fault lie?
The Head Seat replied, "Its fault lies in being within activity. Dongshan then ordered his attendant to remove the fruit table. Dongshan—
At that time, if I had been the Head Seat (Thaisuozuo), when he asked, "Where is it? I would have simply said to him, "Why such a frantic rush?
As soon as he was about to open his mouth, I would have kicked over the fruit table and departed.
Even if Dongshan were at the height of his full capacity, he would still be thirty li behind me.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Xuefeng’s Chan has not a single speck of dust. He merely sees the bell tolling for the assembly to ascend the hall, and thus deceives the multitude into coming up.
Lately there have been tigers in the mountains. Then, letting out a shout, he said: "At this morning of the winter solstice, I speak with inverted words and topsy-turvy phrases."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddha preached the Dharma with a single voice, and sentient beings each understood it according to their own kind.
He then picked up his staff and said, "This mountain monk’s staff has now transformed into Śākyamuni Buddha. He struck the floor once and said, "It is not at all a hindrance for him to speak;
but how do you understand it? If you can understand it, the lanterns will join their palms. If you cannot understand it—"
"The dew-pillar provides proof. [The Master] throws down his staff and descends from the seat.
Entering the hall: "What use can the Patriarchs' Mind-Seal be? The True Person of No-Station is not even worth a drop of excrement.
Striding alone across the azure heavens is merely boasting of skillful hands; blending mud with water—rare indeed is one of the same stream. I dare ask you all: what is the mark of birth?"
"Congratulations! When there is death, one consoles; when one departs, one sees them off; when one enters, one welcomes. What is the single phrase for this?
If you cannot speak it, descend from the seat and go to the various quarters to pay your respects."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Zhaozhou Zen Master addressed the assembly, saying, "Sometimes I take up a blade of grass and make it the sixteen-foot golden body.
Later, Cuoyan remarked, "Old man Zhaozhou deceives the common folk.
If it were Cuoyan, he would have taken up a blade of grass and called it simply "a blade of grass. The Master laughed heartily and said, "He kills people!"
"One must see blood; in acting for others, one must act with thoroughness. These two old fellows—one errs in excessive extravagance, the other errs in excessive parsimony.
You people, a thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing.
He then picked up his staff and said, "Tell me, is this the sixteen-foot golden body, or is it a single blade of grass? Quick! Quick! He threw down the staff and descended from the seat.
The Master was seated.
When Zen Master Xiufeng arrived, he ascended the hall and gave a discourse. He cited the case of Quandaodao, who visited Ciming. Ciming said, "A single cloud spans the mouth of the valley;
from where does the traveler come? Quandaodao looked left and right and said, "Where did the fire come from last night that burned out the old tracks?"
At the Human Grave (Jin-fun), Ming said, "Not yet; speak further and you shall attain it. Quan made the sound of a tiger. Ming struck his sitting mat once.

Quan pushed Ming down to his seat. Ming then made the sound of a tiger. Quan said, "I have studied under seventy-odd spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), but today for the first time I have met a true master (jiazuo).
O Great Assembly, when one encounters a true master on the Great Way, how does that compare to Xuefeng today?"
Meeting a Master of the Way,
he ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said, "The Great Master Yunmen is coming! He struck the ground once with the staff and said,
"The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single fist knocks down the Yellow Crane Tower; a single kick overturns the Parrot Isle. When there is spirit, one adds to that spirit;
where there is no elegance, one is nonetheless elegant. How magnificent! How magnificent! What joy! What joy!
It is like a youth of seventeen or eighteen, acting as if he were the imperial scholar. Who cares for heaven? Who cares for earth?"
The sovereign mind does not move falsely; the six realms are simultaneously penetrated. Lay aside the three-foot sword; cease playing with the single bow. Free and easy, free and easy!
Blissful and joyful, blissful and joyful! It is just like an old man of seventy or eighty serving as a prime minister.
"The winds blow in their season and the rains fall in their season; the five grains flourish and the myriad people are at peace. Then, holding up his staff, he said:
"O assembly, these two, together with this monk’s staff, shall together form a single patch-robed monk.

Upon arriving at the gate of Xuefeng, one simply knows how to follow the custom and eat one's fill; one may also obtain three coins to buy straw sandals. With a shout, he struck the ground with his staff.
[The Master] takes up his staff, descends from his seat, and ascends the hall. He recounts: One day Shushan went to visit Yantou. When Yantou saw him coming, he feigned sleep.
Shushan stood there for a long while, then struck the meditation platform once. Yantou said, "What are you doing? Shushan said, "Master, please stop napping. [He] brushes away [the dust].
Xuexou immediately departed. Yantou said, "For thirty years I have been riding a horse, yet today I have been thrown by a donkey.
Later, Sijian remarked, "Yantou was as impenetrable as a sealed casket, yet he was lightly pressed by Shushan until his defenses crumbled like falling tiles and melting ice.
"Great assembly, you say that the 'great' and 'small' Sijian possessed but a single eye; you do not realize, however, that this hand of Shushan remains hidden."
It was kept within the folds of his sleeves; even the Buddha’s eye could not see it. Yet, when he could no longer restrain himself, he was seen through by a drowsy fellow.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "The dynamic of the 'crack' and the 'peck' is but a temporary livelihood; the principle of pure emptiness must not be relied upon or grasped."
Losing the Way, one will inevitably enter a deviant path. A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a single blow of the staff; the iron ox of Shanfu has both horns broken. I shall not ask further:
regarding this phrase, "Water does not wash water," how would you say it? If you cannot say it—
The fifty-ninth day of the month, once again meeting spring.
Entering the hall: Cutting through with a single stroke—this does not yet suffice for a patch-robed monk. To level the high by following the low is difficult even for a master.
When the ancients reached this point, their mouths were like flat carrying-poles; though it was excellent, there was nonetheless no way out. Xuefeng arrived...
"Right here—how so? After a long silence, he said, "Look in five days.
Upon leaving the monastery, he ascended the hall and took up a bow; he drew an arrow and, with a single casual release, fixed the mountain.
I do not ask you about that. Having cast aside the bow and dropped the arrow, he reached home with hands empty, yet people did not recognize him. The magpies cawed.
"Crows cry among the cypress trees. Again, how is this? "For now, may there be peace throughout the world. Having said this, he returned to the Eastern Hermitage.
Holding a torch, [he said]: "Before the womb was even formed, it was already thus. Once it was formed, from birth through to old age..."
It is thus when one falls ill; it is thus when one reaches death. And now, that the great assembly escorts you and places you upon the Nirvana platform—it is also thus.
Since all three stages are thus, from where could the patriarch’s true essence have come?
Cheshang, it cannot be "thus," nor can it be "not thus. Neither "thus" nor "not thus"—it is not at all.
It can be attained. If you can emerge from this very place with even a single step of realization, who would dare call you a "deceased monk"?
If you have not yet reached this state, your torch is devoid of humanity.
“The deceased monk has passed away; ice returns to water. From where did the Patriarch Zhenjue obtain this news?
“The deceased monk has passed away; water returns to ice. From where did the Dharma Master Xuansha Bei obtain this news?
Right now, I return to you the phrase “ice returning to water,” while setting aside “water returning to ice. Looking at the assembly, he said: “The deceased monk...”
When he passed away, where did he go? If you cannot say, wait until you all become like Elder Caishang, and I will tell you then.
Before Elephant Bone Peak, empty space collapses; atop Black Stone Ridge, the red banner flashes. Upon the Nirvana Terrace lies the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss.

In the hands of this mountain monk is the final stroke: taking a torch, he points to the assembly and then to the deceased monk, saying, "It is right when the eyes are open; it is right when the eyes are closed."
